articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. Details of the specific individuals or entities targeted were not immediately released in the initial announcement.

These designations fall under OFAC's ongoing efforts to disrupt financial support for terrorist organizations globally. Further information regarding the designated parties and the implications of these actions is expected to be published by the Treasury Department.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations with Terror Links
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated several Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations on November 13, 2026, for their involvement in both narcotics trafficking and counter terrorism activities. The designated entities include LOS LORENZANAS, LOS MENDOZA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, and LOS HUISTAS DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION.

LOS LORENZANAS was specifically identified as a Transnational Terrorist Group, while LOS MENDOZA and LOS HUISTAS were linked to Mexican narco-terrorist cartels such as the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion.

These designations expose the organizations to secondary sanctions risk under Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886, aiming to disrupt their financial and logistical support networks.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Sanctions List Entry for Volta Shipping Services
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026, modifying an existing entry on its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. The update pertains to Volta Shipping Services LLC, a UAE-based company previously linked to Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani.
The listed alias for Volta Shipping Services LLC has been changed from Volta Shipping Services FZCO to Volta Container Line FZCO.

The company remains designated under Executive Order 13902 and continues to be subject to secondary sanctions risk, indicating OFAC's ongoing scrutiny of entities involved in Iranian financial channels.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Canada-Based Money Services Businesses for Iran-Related Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026, targeting eight Canada-based money services businesses. These entities are accused of facilitating transactions involving Iran, including converting Iranian currency into digital assets and engaging in transactions with sanctioned Iranian exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' and coordinated with FinCEN and Canada's FINTRAC, was taken under Executive Order 13902.
The designations aim to disrupt international financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions and highlight the increasing focus on digital asset transactions in sanctions enforcement.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Cuba, Cyber, and Transnational Criminal Organizations Sectors
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting entities across cyber-related, transnational criminal organizations, and Cuba-related sectors.

As part of the Cuba designations, OFAC published a determination pursuant to Section 2(a)(i)(A) of Executive Order 14404, specifically targeting the 'Electronics, Manufacturing, Marine, and Technology Sectors of the Cuban Economy.'

The action also included additions to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List for individuals and entities involved in transnational criminal organizations, with some linked to global scam networks and the Prince Group TCO.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, Amends Venezuela GL, and Publishes Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to certain Iran-related listings.
In addition to these designations, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ).
The Iran-related alert and the amended Venezuela GL and FAQ aim to provide further guidance and clarity to the public regarding compliance with U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for International Development Bank
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.'

This amended general license provides a specific authorization for the wind-down of transactions related to the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, indicating a targeted approach to managing existing financial relationships under the Iran sanctions program.

The issuance of such a wind-down license typically allows a limited period for non-U.S. persons to conclude transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, minimizing disruption while maintaining sanctions pressure.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Bank Data Insights

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Sanctions on North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo Entities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

These designations are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to counter threats posed by these regions, including proliferation activities by North Korea and illicit activities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Specific details of the designated parties were not immediately available in the initial announcement.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026, for $1,529,685.

The North Carolina-headquartered cloud networking solutions provider was found to have exported networking equipment and related services on nine occasions between September 2018 and March 2022 to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer.

MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to being majority-owned by the designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey, despite MMZA itself not being directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022. OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Corruption, Crime & Compliance

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, as part of its ongoing review to ensure guidance remains current.
The updated FAQs, specifically numbers 10, 32 through 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, address topics related to blocking and rejecting transactions, as well as filing reports with OFAC.

These revisions clarify when financial institutions must freeze funds, when a transaction should be rejected, and the procedures and deadlines for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions to OFAC.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center

The penalty stems from nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations, involving the export of networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer that was blocked by operation of law.

articles.headline: UK Inflation Rises to 3.6% in October, Fueling Rate Hike Expectations
body: UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October 2026, up from 3.5% in September, reaching its highest level in over a year. The increase was primarily driven by surging petrol and diesel prices, which hit record highs amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and its impact on global oil costs.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) reported that fuel prices saw an annual increase of 33.2%, the largest since July 2022. This rise puts further pressure on the Bank of England to consider another interest rate hike in December, with derivatives markets pricing an 80% chance of such a move.
While core inflation remained steady at 2.8%, energy bills are forecast to rise by 26% in January, indicating continued inflationary pressures on households.

articles.headline: Euro Area Annual Inflation Climbs to 4.0% in October
body: The annual inflation rate in the euro area increased to 4.0% in October 2026, up from 3.8% in September. This marks a significant rise from the 2.1% recorded a year earlier, according to Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union.
Energy prices were the largest contributor to the annual euro area inflation rate, adding 1.89 percentage points. Services also played a substantial role, contributing 1.55 percentage points.
Among member states, Romania recorded the highest annual inflation rate at 7.0%, followed by Lithuania at 6.1% and Bulgaria at 5.9%. Conversely, Sweden had the lowest rate at 0.6%.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
